summary:
FirePulse: Satellite-Powered Fire Activity Intelligence
FirePulse is a web application that combines NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations into one consistent picture of fire activity. The two sensors differ in resolution (1 km for MODIS, 375 m for VIIRS) and in how they report detection confidence, so their raw counts can’t be compared directly. FirePulse harmonizes them and presents the result as a unified burning activity calendar, with Kerala, India as the initial region of focus.

What it does

Shows MODIS and VIIRS hotspots on an interactive map.
Harmonizes the two datasets by converting both confidence scales to a common low/nominal/high scale and rescaling VIIRS counts to MODIS-equivalent units. Both are then averaged into a single daily activity index.
Compares raw and harmonized MODIS and VIIRS detections side by side.
Presents fire activity as daily, weekly and monthly calendars.
Shows historical patterns, such as the yearly fire season, by year and month.
Flags unusually high fire days by comparing each day with its trailing 30-day baseline.

Who it helps

Researchers can study long-term fire patterns, emergency responders can see critical periods, and land managers can plan around the fire season.

How it was built

Python, Streamlit, Pandas, Folium and Plotly, using NASA FIRMS data (MODIS and VIIRS active fire).
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

FirePulse is a web application that combines NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS active-fire data into one consistent view of fire activity. MODIS (1 km resolution) and VIIRS (375 m resolution) detect fires differently and report confidence differently, so their raw counts can’t be compared directly. FirePulse loads hotspot data from NASA FIRMS and converts both sensors’ confidence values to a common low/nominal/high scale. It then rescales VIIRS counts to MODIS-equivalent units using the ratio of total detections, and averages the two into a single daily activity index. From this index it produces:

  • an interactive map of hotspots
  • a MODIS vs VIIRS comparison chart
  • daily, weekly and monthly activity calendars
  • historical year-by-month patterns
  • flags for unusually high fire days, found by comparing each day with its trailing 30-day baseline

We focused first on Kerala, India.

What benefits does it have?

It gives researchers a single, comparable record of fire activity instead of two incompatible datasets. Emergency responders and land managers can see at a glance when the fire season peaks and which days were unusual. It is easy to use, since it runs in a browser and needs no GIS expertise.

What is the intended impact?

We want to turn raw satellite observations into clear, usable information that supports environmental monitoring, fire-season planning and disaster preparedness. The method is not specific to Kerala, so it could be applied to any region covered by FIRMS.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Language: Python
  • Libraries: Streamlit (web app), Pandas and NumPy (data processing), Folium (maps), Plotly (charts), Requests (FIRMS API)
  • Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS active fire data)
  • Software: GitHub for code hosting, Windows PowerShell
  • Hardware: a standard laptop (no special hardware)

How is your project creative?

Rather than showing the two sensors separately, we combined them into one unified activity index and used it to build a fire calendar, which makes the sensors easy to compare and read. We also put the harmonization, calendars, historical patterns and anomaly detection into one simple interface that non-experts can use.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Sensor differences: resolution (1 km vs 375 m), detection sensitivity and confidence scales
  • Data quality: users can filter out low-confidence detections
  • Usability: a single browser interface with simple tabs for different users
  • Data size: long date ranges produce large files, so the app limits how many points are drawn on the map
  • Limitations: our rescaling uses a simple overall ratio, which is a basic approximation. Future versions could use more advanced calibration, other regions and live alerts.
